Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I distract myself with something else
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Samuel stood in the doorway of his study, the late afternoon light catching the dust motes over the unrolled Torah. He was sixty-three now, but the corridor of those years had not closed. He remembered the night the road changed, when the men in the checkpoints moved with sudden hands, when a baton flashed against his forearm, when a rifle strap caught his collar, and when voices rose into a wall of shouts that swallowed every plea. He did not need to write it down for anyone; the memory lived in the way his shoulders still hunched when a colleague patted his back without warning, in the way his breath caught when a stack of files was dropped on his desk and the leather strap caught his wrist, in the way the synagogue courtyard still felt dangerous when someone’s voice climbed too quickly above the rest. The past had been a long stretch of borders and thresholds, where anything could be taken and anyone could speak over him. That was why the present day still held so many silent alarms. His body continued to react as though the corridor were still open, even when the sanctuary doors were shut and the air was still. He had grown certain he could not trust his own steadiness when the room felt crowded or the air grew thick. He chose his seat in the study by the far window, where the frame covered his shoulder, and only felt safe in the rear office or the far corner of the study, nowhere else. Shouts in the courtyard sent his attention elsewhere; he found himself folding a tallit or reorganizing a stack of sermons, letting the task absorb his focus. The habit formed slowly, then held fast. Guilt had its own quiet shape. He found himself replaying the nights they were turned back at the river, certain that if only someone stronger had pushed past the officers, the course would have shifted. He carried that weight now as a ledger he felt he had earned: he deserved the strain of waking before dawn to draft the shiva list, deserved the ache in his shoulders from carrying the extra crates, deserved the long silences at his own table. When his partner reached across the breakfast counter to rest a hand on his, he stepped back, telling himself that closeness only deepened the vulnerability he could not afford. He had built a quiet distance into their years together, preferring separate rooms, separate schedules, separate prayers. The congregation noticed only that he had become more reserved, that he no longer stayed after services for the long conversations he once welcomed. His pulpit notes had grown shorter, the margins lined with careful calculations of building repairs rather than the expansive midrashim he used to write. For weeks now, the strain had made its way into his preparation. He sat at the study desk, the parchment unrolled, but his eyes could not hold the line. He watched the ink blur and knew his thoughts were scattering, that the words were passing through him without settling. He had come to understand that his own mind was a place he could no longer rely on to hold what he needed to say. His partner had asked him to speak to someone, not as a counselor but as a man who carried a heavy yoke. He had come because the quiet distances had begun to feel like walls, because he feared he was teaching from a place of absence rather than presence. He did not expect the memories to leave him, but he hoped, quietly, that the alarms might finally learn the difference between the past and the room he was sitting in now.
